opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what we actually want intelligence to do. A lot of the progress we've seen in AI has been in domains like language and images, where the system takes in data and produces some output, but it never really has to act in the world and live with the consequences of those actions. When you think about human intelligence, or animal intelligence more broadly, so much of it is grounded in interacting with a physical environment: picking things up, moving around, predicting what will happen when you push something or pour water into a cup.

That kind of interaction gives you a very different and, I'd argue, much richer form of understanding. If you only learn from passive data, you can pick up a lot of statistical correlations, but it's much harder to learn causal structure, to know what happens if I do this versus that. Embodiment forces you to build models of the world that are actually predictive, because if your model is wrong, the robot drops the cup or bumps into the wall. That feedback loop is incredibly valuable.

There's also a practical side. Many of the most impactful applications of AI, in the home, in manufacturing, in healthcare, in science, involve physical tasks. If we want AI systems that can actually help people in their daily lives, they need to operate in the physical world, deal with uncertainty, generalize to new objects and environments, and plan over long horizons.

So for me, embodiment isn't just one application area for AI. It's a lens on what intelligence really requires: perception, reasoning, planning, and action all working together. A lot of my research, for example on generative models as world models and on composing models to solve new tasks, is motivated by that idea: building systems that can imagine the consequences of their actions and use that to act intelligently in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response frames embodiment as part of what intelligence requires and says AI systems must operate in the physical world to act intelligently there.

r002.rationale: It gives a robot dropping a cup or bumping into a wall as an example of an AI system learning through physical interaction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that so much of what we call intelligence was shaped by having to act in the world. Humans and animals didn't develop reasoning in a vacuum; we developed it because we had to move, manipulate things, predict what happens when we push on something, and recover when we're wrong. Those pressures are what gave rise to our ability to plan, to build models of cause and effect, and to generalize to situations we've never seen before.

When you look at the large language models today, they're remarkable, but they've learned from a very particular slice of experience: text that humans wrote down. And text is a kind of compressed, lossy summary of the world. People don't write down the things that are obvious to anyone with a body, like the fact that a cup will fall if you let go of it, or that you need to grip a wet object differently than a dry one. So these systems inherit a lot of our conclusions without ever having access to the underlying process that produced them. That shows up as the brittleness we see when you ask them about physical situations, or when you try to get them to actually control a robot.

Embodiment matters because it closes the loop. When an agent takes an action and then observes the consequence, it gets a signal that's grounded in reality rather than in what someone said about reality. That's the kind of feedback that lets you build genuine world models, where you can imagine, "if I do this, then that will happen," and check yourself. A lot of my own work has been on exactly that: learning generative models of how the world evolves, and then using them for planning. And what I've found is that the models that work best are the ones that can be corrected by interaction. You can't get that purely from passive data.

I'd also say there's a scientific argument, not just an engineering one. If we want to understand intelligence as a phenomenon, we should take seriously that every intelligent system we know of is embodied. That doesn't mean a robot arm is the only path forward, and I don't think a model needs to be a humanoid to be smart. But I do think the ability to perceive, act, and observe consequences in some environment, even a simulated one, is probably a prerequisite for the kind of robust, common-sense reasoning we actually want, rather than something you can bolt on at the end.

r001.rationale: The response says interaction with an environment is a prerequisite, but explicitly allows that environment to be simulated. It does not clearly assert that physical embodiment in the world is necessary.

r002.rationale: It describes AI systems controlling robots and identifies a robot arm as one possible path for embodied intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think embodiment is important because it gives an intelligent system a way to learn through interaction. When you read text or look at images, you’re observing what happened. When you act in the world, you can ask a different kind of question: If I do this, what changes? You can test your predictions and learn from the consequences.

For example, an object might look easy to pick up, but actually grasping it requires understanding its weight, its friction, and how it responds to contact. A lot of that knowledge is difficult to acquire from appearance alone. It comes from acting, getting feedback, and adjusting.

I wouldn’t say every useful AI system needs a physical body. But if we want systems that understand the physical world and can reliably help us in it, interaction is a crucial part of that. Embodiment connects what a system perceives to what it can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response says not every useful AI system needs a physical body; it describes embodiment as crucial for systems that understand and act in the physical world, not as necessary for AI generally.

r002.rationale: The response discusses acting and interacting in the world but does not identify robotics as an instantiation of physically intelligent AI agents.

sol-6.1.text:
I think embodiment is important because it connects intelligence to the consequences of actions. You can learn a tremendous amount from text and images, but those are largely observations of what other people have done. When you interact with the world, you can ask questions through action: If I push this object, what happens? If I try something and it fails, how should I change my approach?

That interaction helps you learn about causality, physics, and how to achieve goals under uncertainty. Even a simple task like picking up a cup requires combining perception, prediction, and control, then adjusting as you get new feedback.

I wouldn’t say every useful AI system needs a physical body. But if we want intelligence that can understand and operate in the physical world, I think learning through interaction is a crucial part of that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says not every useful AI system needs a physical body and limits the need for interaction to AI that operates in the physical world; it does not assert embodiment is necessary for AI generally.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses physical interaction and a cup-picking task but does not identify robotics as an instantiation of physically intelligent AI agents.
